A Third Pair of Eyes?

AI-Assisted Review of Statistical Reports and Code

Author

Valentin Klotzbücher · DKF Basel

Updated

22 November 2026

The handout to the talk, to read later: what two studies found this autumn, three ways to get an AI review of a statistical product, why building more tools may not pay, the questions for the discussion, and a test case to try the tools on. A statistical product here is a sample size estimation, an analysis plan or a report, and the review covers all of it: the statistical methods, the numbers and the code.

Each of the three ways has a starter in the kit, github.com/valentinklotzbuecher/scto-ai-review: a prompt to paste and a skill for the chat, my review prototype as a Quarto document for the API, and the review skills for the agent, still in development; and there is a list of review services. It is my own exploration, not a DKF service or recommendation.

Models find more errors than reviewers did

In the largest experiment of its kind, Schroter and colleagues gave 607 reviewers of a general medical journal three reports of randomised trials with 9 major and 5 minor errors inserted (BMJ 2004; J R Soc Med 2008). This autumn, Brian et al. gave the same three reports to 15 language models, without tools or web access, and scored every review against the same answer key. The human reviewers had found 27% of the major errors. Every model found more: 53% (Haiku 4.5) to 96% (Opus 5.5). On 58 trials published in 2026, with the same kinds of error inserted, the models found 46% to 93%.

The caveats, from the preprint: the human comparison is historical; language models judged the reviews; models that found more inserted errors also flagged more problems in unmodified reports (specificity 82% overall); four of the authors are affiliated with a foundation whose platform is implementing AI-assisted review. And the authors draw the boundary of the design themselves:

Every error tested here is visible in the text, whereas errors in data handling or analysis code, undisclosed deviations from the registered protocol and fabricated data are not.

The same week, King and Worthington compared AI reviews with paid human reviews of 124 submissions, reviews that editors and authors had rated unusually good. One review per paper from Claude Opus 4.8 at its maximum reasoning setting, given the manuscript and the reviewer guidelines, was better “by every measure we could construct”; three former journal editors preferred it in 26 of 30 judgments. It is a working paper, too.

The preprint’s last author, Ruslan Rust, on X:

From now on I won’t do any peer review without AI. For clinical trials, I’d even call human-only review dangerous.

So the question is less whether to use these tools than how.

Internal consistency review

Sample size estimations, analysis plans and reports go to a second statistician, who checks the methods, the numbers and the code. Both studies read only the text; errors in data handling or analysis code, the preprint’s authors note, are not visible there. Where could AI come in: before the second statistician, as a check the author runs first, or alongside the reviewer? That is open. The three approaches below are what I explored, as a basis for the discussion.

Three approaches

The chat; a script through the API, here my review prototype, with the review services, someone else’s pipeline, as templates for developing it further; and, after a dividing line, an agent that runs the code in the repository. Skills, your checklist as a folder, come up twice: in the chat, and as the agent’s instructions.

01Paste it into the chat

Choose the strongest model your plan offers at its maximum reasoning setting (ChatGPT’s Pro series, Claude Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.2), attach the PDF and the Quarto source, and ask whether it is consistent. In my experience this has worked well since OpenAI’s o1 pro, in December 2024, and King and Worthington’s AI reviews were made this way. What you don’t get: a record of what was checked, the same answer twice, or any code run.

You can also give the chat your own checklist, as a skill: a folder you upload once and then name in your request.

Please review this using /dkf-document-check.

What its SKILL.md holds:

  • Rules: only cleared documents; the print decides; no product code runs.
  • 1 Documents and versions: is it what it says, and does it match the protocol, the SAP, the registry entry?
  • 2 Printed numbers: do they agree and add up? Each is recomputed by a script.
  • 3 Design, estimand and method: do they answer the question the product states?
  • Output: findings, a consistency table, a check log.

Next to it: references/ (estimands, clinical guidelines, product profiles) and scripts/recompute.py. The model reads only the names and descriptions of its skills until a request matches, then loads the rest. dkf-document-check is the first stage of my review skills on its own; it runs no product code. My skills are adapted from research_skills, released by Joe Francis.

Starter: tools/1-chat: the prompt, the settings, the skill, the data rules

02An API review prototype

Instead of pasting by hand, a script: my review prototype, a Quarto document that sends the product through the API. It takes the product’s Quarto source and its PDF. Its chunks hold the settings, in R; the prompt, from a text file; and the request, sent with the Anthropic Python SDK through reticulate. ellmer could send it too; the SDK gives the exact stop reason and lets the document check that the model read the whole source. One request per run, paid per use with an API key, under the API’s terms. Every run is saved as Markdown and JSON, with its settings, its tokens and hashes of the prompt and the inputs, and never overwritten. Rendering the document shows the latest review, with the prompt and the cost. The price is code that talks to one provider at one point in time.

How it is set up, in the kit’s tools/2-api:

  1. Put the product’s .qmd and PDF in to_be_reviewed/.

  2. Set cfg in the first chunk, runtime-params: the files, the assignment (the questions the review must answer), the model and its effort.

    cfg <- list(
  review_folder    = "to_be_reviewed",
  qmd_file         = "DEMO-TKA_SSE.qmd",
  pdf_file         = "DEMO-TKA_SSE.pdf",
  assignment       = "Is the sample size right?",
  anthropic_model  = "claude-opus-5-5",
  anthropic_effort = "max"
)

  3. Edit prompt.md if you like: a senior biostatistician’s first pass, with a checklist for each product type (sample size estimation, analysis report, data preparation).

  4. Run the chunks runtime-params, setup-r and setup-py, then anthropic-review-manual, which sends the request. It is eval=FALSE: rendering never sends anything.

  5. Render: the latest review, the prompt as sent and the cost.

What the review looks like is set in prompt.md, and yours to change. A run whose model did not confirm reading the whole source is marked not completed.

And because it is a script, you can test it: run it on test cases with known answers and score every run. In R, the vitals package does this with ellmer; it is a port of Inspect, a Python framework for evaluating language models. So you can compare prompts, models and effort settings on cases you know, such as the demo below.

Starter: tools/2-api: review.qmd, prompt.md and the folder to_be_reviewed/

Further development: review services as templates

Others have built such pipelines, with many more calls, and offer them as services; for a script of your own, they are templates. You upload the PDF, a fixed chain of model calls with prompts the vendor wrote runs behind it, and you get a report. Refine (refine.ink), the oldest, founded by the Northwestern economist Benjamin Golub and Yann Calvó López, is seen as the gold standard and costs up to $50 a review; reviewer3.com is paid too; paperreview.ai from Stanford, openaireview.org from Chicago and Google’s Deep Review (two reviews a week) are free; and two are open source: coarse.ink, apparently reverse-engineered from Refine, and Joe Francis’s Reviewer 2. Reviewer 2 chains more than 30 model calls, which take 15–45 minutes and cost a few dollars: its first stage, The Breaker, takes “a sledgehammer to academic texts”, and a verification cascade removes what the aggression invents. All are built for research papers, and all but the open-source ones mean uploading to a third party. I was planning to fork Reviewer 2, to improve it or to learn from it for my own script.

Starter: tools/services: the list, with links and sources

The bitter lesson

… general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin.

Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson, 2019

On 26 October Joe Francis retired the hosted Reviewer 2, which he had decided was obsolete: “Something better and free coming shortly.” The same day he released the three skills he begins his reviews with: “Point your agent at a folder with an article, its supplementary material, and replication package, and it will assess it”; a second skill verifies the review, a third writes a digest. Hand-built machinery keeps losing to general methods that use more computation, and review tools are no exception; on the day Google launched Deep Review, Rex Douglass wrote that for about three years he had thought about building such a tool at least twice a day, and didn’t, because “one of the big three does it and it’s over”. So how much more to build, when tools become obsolete this fast? My skills, which the agent below follows, are adapted from Francis’s. My own prototype dates with every new model, and my skills will too.

What carries over to every new model:

  • test cases with known answers, to see what a tool finds and what it misses;
  • standards for what a review must check;
  • rules for what data may go where.

A shared set of test cases, written by different people and kept out of every review, would let anyone measure any tool, and every new model; the demo is a first one.

03In development: agentic review

What I did based on that: a coding agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, with my skills, adapted from Joe Francis’s, as its instructions. Here Claude Code on the web, which works in an isolated cloud VM with the product’s repository and the review skills. You type one sentence. The agent decides the next step, with its model, which runs at the provider; its tools read files, run R and write logs, and the result goes back, until it is done; the review and its logs are pushed to a branch.

It never touches your computer, and it runs on your Claude plan, without API credits; what it reads still goes to the provider. The same agent can be started from a script, with the Agent SDK in Python or TypeScript, or with claude -p from R: to run it over test cases with known answers, for batch runs, with guardrails in code. That runs on an API key, billed per token, and one review does not need it.

What it adds over the script:

  • It runs the code: it re-renders the product, recomputes the printed numbers and re-runs the simulations.
  • It challenges its findings: an agent that did not write a finding checks it, in a fresh context.
  • Synthetic data when patient data cannot be shared: dummy data built from the code or from a codebook made locally, so the code runs. It shows that the code runs and does what the text says, never a printed number.
  • Version-controlled: every script, log and result is committed with the product, so it could become part of its replication package; REVIEW comments go into a copy of the .qmd.

Still in development. The skills are at version 0.3.1, tested so far on one synthetic test case, the demo, where every run found all six planted issues.

Starter: tools/3-agent: the set-up, the one sentence, the depth and the data modes; the skills are in stats_review, version 0.3.1

Try it yourself

The skill, in a chat. Download dkf-document-check.zip from stats_review’s chat-skills/ and upload it in Claude (Customize, then Skills, then “+”; code execution must be on). In a new chat, attach the product’s PDF and its Quarto source, and ask:

Please review this using /dkf-document-check.

It runs on your Claude plan; the steps are in the kit’s tools/1-chat.

The review document is in the kit, scto-ai-review, in the folder tools/2-api. With an API key in ~/.Renviron:

  1. Put the product in to_be_reviewed/; for the demo, from the kit’s top folder:

    cp demo/sse/DEMO-TKA_SSE.qmd demo/sse/DEMO-TKA_SSE.pdf tools/2-api/to_be_reviewed/

  2. Open review.qmd in RStudio, set cfg, run the chunks, and render.

Every run is kept in review_results/prototype_runs/.

The agent, still in development, runs on the review skills in stats_review, at the tag skills-v0.3.1; the steps are in the kit’s tools/3-agent.

  1. At claude.ai/code, on your Claude plan, create a cloud environment with stats_review’s tools/web_setup.sh as its setup script; it installs R and Quarto.

  2. Start a session with your product’s repository and stats_review.

  3. Type one sentence:

    Review the product with dkf-review, then write the consistency review.

  4. The review lands on a branch of your product’s repository; merge it there.

Start with the demo: a two-page sample size estimation with six planted issues and an answer key.

Questions to discuss

The preprint’s last author won’t review without AI any more, and calls human-only review dangerous for clinical trials. And AI-only review?

  1. How should AI complement our review? For whom: the author, as a check before the second statistician, the reviewer, alongside the review, or both? And how deep: one call that reads, or an agent that runs everything? One reason to want it: a single reviewer sees only part of what more reviewers would raise. In the NeurIPS 2021 reviews, one reviewer raised about a fifth of the issues that all of a paper’s reviewers raised together (Liu, Guo, Hartline and Hullman, 2026); an AI that applies the same checks to every product takes some of the luck out of who reviews it.
  2. Review results, not lines? In a result-oriented review the AI goes through every line, every number and every re-run, and keeps its tests and logs. The human checks that the AI tested enough, that each chunk, section, preparation step and analysis does what it says, and that the approach and the interpretation hold. Even the author of the skills mine build on says: “When using them, you should remember that the results have been produced by robots and should be verified by humans” (Joe Francis on X, 26 October 2026). A caution: the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 62% of their review weaknesses from the appendix, human reviewers about 8%; they audit every detail and rarely engage with the core of the paper. The authors’ advice: use them “as a tool for checking the details, not as the judge of what matters most in a paper” (Ghosh, Saim and Jiang, 2026).
  3. What would you need to see before you sign a product an AI reviewed?

Thinking further ahead

  1. A checklist learned from our past reviews? Liu and colleagues turned a corpus of past reviews into a checklist of criticisms: with language-model reviewers it cut the error of a three-reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and in a study with 20 people it lowered the error of a paper ranking from 0.48 to 0.22. Could our archive of review forms become such a checklist, for the human reviewer and the AI alike?
  2. A replication certificate with every product? Certify, from Gary King, Yiqing Xu and Leo Yang at Harvard (a beta), has your own AI assistant, such as Claude Code or Codex, rerun a replication package on your computer; the certificate adds “evidence that rerunning the code produces the results to be published.”
  3. Implications for teaching? If the AI does the line work, how will junior statisticians learn to review? How do we train our staff, and how fast should we adopt?
  4. Build our own tools, or wait for the next model? See the bitter lesson above: what carries over is test cases, review standards and data rules.
  5. Should we write our products for AI readers? The estimand in full, every assumption in the text and not only in the code, every number traceable to the code that makes it?

The demo

DEMO-TKA is a synthetic sample size estimation of two pages (app-guided home exercise versus supervised physiotherapy after total knee arthroplasty) with six planted issues: two visible in the text, two only in the source code, and two that need a calculation or a re-run. Try it yourself first, then with a tool, giving the tool only the two files in demo/sse/.

The agent with the review skills, in three recorded runs:

Date Depth Planted issues found Consequence stated Time Cost at API list prices
31 Oct 2026 standard 6 of 6 5 of 5 202 min of model time about $72
3 Nov 2026 standard, modules skipped, interim 6 of 6 5 of 5 98 min of active time $26.84
5 Nov 2026 quick 6 of 6 5 of 5 34 min, start to final form $9.72

All three ran on a subscription; the costs are what the same tokens cost through the API. Five of the six issues have a consequence in participants or power. Not a blind test: the skills and the demo were written in the same week, and the skills already describe two of the planted issue types. The chat with the skill also found all six and stated the five consequences (20 November 2026), running only its own scripts. Runs of the chat on its own and of the review document are still to do.

WarningSpoilers: the six planted issues
# Level Issue
1 Text Dropout inflation multiplies by 1.2 instead of dividing by 0.8
2 Text The estimand names no intercurrent events and no strategies for them
3 Code The simulation tests one-sided; the text and Table 1 state a two-sided 5% level
4 Code The baseline–outcome correlation that drives the ANCOVA gain appears only in the code, unstated and unsourced
5 Computation Figure 1 plots a running maximum of noisy estimates, and the sample size is the first grid point where that maximum crosses 80%
6 Computation The typed t-test comparison (94 per group) is not what the code computes (105)

What the planning values support: with the stated two-sided 5% level the ANCOVA needs 80 evaluable participants per group, and with 20% loss to follow-up 100 per group, 200 in total, against the SSE’s 132. As planned, the trial has about 62% power for the two-sided test.

The quick run’s review, the first lines (the 5 November run, demo/runs/2026-11-05_agent/):

One finding, traced: the first version of the key said 79 per group, treating the baseline as fixed. The agent’s first review said 80: it computed the power with a random baseline, as the SSE simulates it, and the chance difference in baseline means costs about half a participant per group. The agent was right, and the key was corrected.

Data rules

  • Everything a tool reads goes to the provider: chat, API, service and agent alike. The terms of your plan, the API or the service decide what happens to it.
  • On personal plans (Pro, Max), whether chats may be used for model training is a privacy setting; commercial plans and the API are not covered by the consumer terms.
  • A service is a third party: read its terms before you upload anything unpublished.
  • No patient-level data without a recorded clearance. The agent’s data modes make this explicit: none (documents and code), synthetic (dummy data built from the code) and shared (patient-level data, with the clearance recorded before the run).
  • Check your institution’s rules first.
